claims.text: Constituent count alone does not control the mechanical-property differences; the chemical and magnetic identities of the elements are important.
CrCoNi has superior strength and plastic deformation compared with equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
Thermomechanically processed equiatomic CrCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi can both have an initially single-phase FCC structure.
CrCoNi has an HCP structure with lower energy than its FCC structure.
Plastic deformation can trigger an FCC-to-HCP transformation in CrCoNi.
The FCC-to-HCP transformation in CrCoNi is triggered by dislocation slip and interactions with internal boundaries.
Magnetic frustration associated with Mn removes or obscures the FCC-HCP energetic driving force in CrMnFeCoNi.
The absence of Mn in CrCoNi lowers its stacking-fault energy relative to CrMnFeCoNi.
The absence of Mn lowers the energy barrier for deformation-twin formation in CrCoNi.
CrCoNi forms deformation-induced nanotwins more readily than CrMnFeCoNi.
The HCP nanophase and deformation twins interact with dislocations and thereby enhance work hardening.
The HCP nanophase and deformation twins enhance ductility in CrCoNi.
CrMnFeCoNi undergoes negligible FCC-to-HCP transformation compared with CrCoNi under comparable deformation.
CrMnFeCoNi develops a lower deformation-twin density than CrCoNi.
The transformation mechanism can increase strength without compromising plastic deformation in CrCoNi.
Under identical deformation conditions, CrCoNi will exhibit a larger measurable HCP fraction than CrMnFeCoNi.
Under identical deformation conditions, CrCoNi will exhibit greater work hardening and ductility than CrMnFeCoNi.
A related equiatomic quaternary alloy should show the same higher twin density, HCP fraction, work hardening, and ductility predicted for CrCoNi.
Cryogenic temperature and controlled strain rate promote twinning or phase transformation in low-stacking-fault-energy alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits twins and/or an HCP phase as alternative mediators, but the falsification rule says that failure to observe either a higher twin density or an HCP transformation is sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. Under the stated 'and/or' mechanism, absence of one marker should not be decisive if the other marker and its mechanical association are observed.
